title: agape: the word for love that isn't a feeling
hook: agape: the word for love that isn't a feeling
carry: love is what you do when you don't feel it
tomorrow: why the symbol is an execution device

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Beatitudes. The upside-down list that starts at the bottom. Your line: the last shall be first. Did you let someone go first? Day thirteen.

If you've been to a wedding, you've probably heard today's reading. Someone's cousin stands up, a little nervous, and reads: love is patient, love is kind. It's on cards. On mugs. On the wall above somebody's couch. It's so familiar it sounds soft. Here's the surprise. It wasn't written for a wedding. It was written to a church that was falling apart. People taking each other to court. Splitting into camps behind their favorite teachers. Showing off who was more spiritual. Paul had started that church, in the Greek city of Corinth, and he wrote them a letter. And in the middle of all the scolding, he stopped and wrote this. Today's word is the one he chose.
screen: `LOVE IS PATIENT, LOVE IS KIND.` → `NOT WRITTEN FOR A WEDDING.` → `WRITTEN TO A CHURCH IN A FIGHT.`

segments.voice: Love. English has one word for it. You love your mother, your dog, pizza, a song. Greek had several. Eros, the love that wants. Philia, the love between friends. And the one Paul chose, the one the New Testament leans on more than any other: agape. The noun was rare in older Greek. The first Christians made it their word, and they filled it with a particular meaning: love as a choice, not a mood. Love that acts for someone's good whether or not you feel warm about them. Now listen to how Paul describes it, in the King James Bible: "Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up." Charity. That's the old translation's word. It comes from the Latin caritas, which is related to the word for dear, even costly. Today charity sounds like a donation box, so newer Bibles say love. But the old word tells you something: this is love with its sleeves rolled up. Notice something else. Almost every line in the passage is a verb. Suffers long. Is kind. Doesn't envy. Doesn't brag. Paul isn't describing a feeling. He's describing behavior, the kind you could watch someone do. That's why it fit a church full of people who didn't like each other. He wasn't asking them to feel warm. He was asking them to be patient, and kind, and to stop showing off. He ends: "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity." Christians say this is how God loves first. Another letter puts it simply: "We love him, because he first loved us." On an ordinary Tuesday, agape is the text you send to the friend who's been hard to be around.
screen: `GREEK HAD SEVERAL WORDS.` · `AGAPE — LOVE AS A CHOICE.` · `CHARITY — LOVE WITH SLEEVES UP.` · `EVERY LINE IS A VERB.` · then, large: `THE GREATEST OF THESE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and breathe out slowly. Now think of someone who's hard to love right now. Not the hardest person in your life. Someone mildly difficult. A coworker. A relative. A roommate. You don't have to feel anything warm. Just picture them, and ask one plain question: what would be kind, for them, today? Something small you could actually do. Let an answer come, or don't. Then just breathe. Forty-five seconds. The bell holds the time.
Love. In Greek, agape: love that's a choice, not a mood. The King James calls it charity. Thirteenth word.
Your line: love is what you do when you don't feel it. Today, do the small kind thing for the person you pictured. Don't wait until you feel like it. Day thirteen.

howItsDone: Christians often read 1 Corinthians 13 at weddings and funerals, and many describe agape as the love God shows first and asks people to show each other, in what they do more than in what they feel.

a demand that the troublemakers leave.
fork.reveal: "charity suffereth long, and is kind." the most famous love passage ever written was sent to people in a fight.

original.note: Greek. love that chooses someone's good. the New Testament's main word for love.

trapdoor: what you thought: love is the warm feeling from the wedding reading.
what it means: agape — love as a choice, something you do for someone's good.
what a scholar hears: the noun was rare in older Greek; Christians made it theirs. the Latin Bible said caritas, and the King James turned that into "charity."
